mainKeyword: best rv air conditioner with heat pump
guideTitle: Best RV Air Conditioners with Heat Pumps (2026)
metaTitle: Best RV Air Conditioners with Heat Pumps (2026)
metaDescription: Six RV air conditioners with real heat pumps compared on heating BTU, defrost behavior, 115V versus 12V and 48V power, and cold-air limits.
expertTake: The Gidrox 13,500 BTU 115V heat pump is the sensible choice for a 21 to 25 foot trailer, with 12,000 BTU of quoted heating from a unit that is sized for the rig. The TOSOT 16K is the quieter big-rig option. Skip a heat pump as your cold-camp plan: below freezing the quoted heat figure is a fond memory and a furnace does the work.
introParagraphs: A heat pump keeps an RV warm by running its refrigeration cycle backward, pulling heat from the outside air and releasing it indoors. When the outdoor air is mild, it delivers several units of heat for each unit of electricity, which makes it far more efficient than a resistive element.

That advantage shrinks as the weather cools. The colder it gets, the less heat there is to move, and the unit spends more time in defrost cycles to clear ice from the outdoor coil. We rank each pick by the heating it quotes, how it handles cold air and what it asks of the electrical system.

products.name: Gidrox 13,500 BTU 115V RV AC with heat pump, 43 dB claim
products.description:
Gidrox sizes this heat pump for 21 to 25 foot trailers, pairing 13,500 BTU of cooling with a quoted 12,000 BTU of heating. The heating figure is close to the cooling figure, which is what a genuine heat pump should deliver in mild weather and a rarity in a market full of units with a token heat function.

The maker says the heat pump saves about 65 percent of the energy of a standard heater, a comparison against resistive heat that fits the physics of reverse-cycle heating. A dual-sided outlet with a 100 degree adjustment range spreads air widely, and a claimed 43 dB suits sleeping. Airflow is listed at 330 CFM.

As always, the heating output declines as the outdoor temperature falls, and the unit is fixed to a 115V supply. Compared with the TOSOT it is smaller and better matched to modest trailers. Wash the filter monthly and watch the drainage in cold weather.

products.name: TOSOT 16,000 BTU RV AC heat pump, 43 dB claim, black
products.description:
TOSOT positions the heat pump on this 16,000 BTU unit for the transition seasons, spring and fall, when firing the furnace is overkill. It quotes 12,500 BTU of heating and says the unit works across a wide range of ambient temperatures, a claim to read as a limit and not a promise.

The 43 dB sound claim, which the maker says is 32 percent quieter than a standard RV unit, is the headline for a large unit. In a big trailer or a motorhome bedroom, that quiet is the reason to pay a premium. The black shroud suits dark roof trim.

Versus the Gidrox it has more cooling capacity and a slightly stronger heating figure for a bigger rig. A fixed-speed compressor means a soft start is wise on a generator. Check the roof gasket annually and wash the filter monthly.

products.name: 15,000 BTU 12V RV AC with 1,650W electric heat, 800 CFM
products.description:
This listing combines a heat pump label, a 1,650 watt electric heating element and an automatic defrost function for cold-weather operation, with a quoted 800 CFM of airflow, the highest in this guide. The defrost feature matters because a heat pump in cool damp air builds frost on its outdoor coil.

The listing mixes terms, so read the specification sheet before buying: a 15,000 BTU unit with a 12V label and a 1,650 watt element draws far more than a typical 12V system can supply, so confirm the actual power input. The airflow figure suggests a strong fan in a large cabin, and the element gives a reliable backup in colder air.

Where the Gidrox is concerned, this one offers an electric backup and airflow, but the electrical story is less clear. Check wiring and documentation before buying, and keep the coil and drain clear.

products.name: Gidrox 12,000 BTU 48V DC RV AC with heat pump
products.description:
Forty-eight volts is the interesting number: a 48V system draws a quarter of the current of a 12V system for the same power, so cables are thin and voltage drop is small. Gidrox pairs that with a heat pump quoting 11,000 BTU of heating and 12,000 BTU of cooling, and says the sleep mode uses only 300 watts overnight.

The maker says the heat pump saves about 75 percent of the energy of a standard heater, and runs from the battery with no inverter. A brushless fan and sound insulation give a quoted 40 dB in sleep mode. The catch is obvious: you need a 48V battery system, which is common in some high-end conversions and bus builds but unusual in a standard trailer.

Compared with the 115V Gidrox it trades shore power for battery independence. Wire it per the maker's sheet, use a proper fuse and a low-voltage cutoff, and check terminals each season.

products.name: 15,000 BTU 115V RV AC with heat, dual-rotary compressor, R32
products.description:
A dual-rotary compressor uses two rotors that balance each other, reducing vibration and allowing smoother operation than a single-rotor type. This 115V unit pairs that with R32 refrigerant and an airflow of 500 cubic meters per hour, a large figure for a rooftop box.

The maker says it works directly with campground power and household power and offers one-click switching between Fahrenheit and Celsius. At 15,000 BTU it covers mid-size and larger trailers, and the heat function gives warmth in mild weather. The listing gives little on heating capacity or noise, so check the sheet.

Compared with the TOSOT it has a more sophisticated compressor on paper but less published detail. A fixed-speed rating is not stated, so ask about startup current. Wash the filter and check the roof seal yearly.

products.name: Arsenda 18,000 BTU rooftop RV AC with heat pump, 50 dB
products.description:
Arsenda's 18,000 BTU unit is the biggest heat pump in the guide, with a quoted 50 dB and a standard non-ducted fit. It is aimed at large trailers and fifth wheels that want capacity and mild-weather heat for less than an established brand costs.

The unit needs both 115V AC and 12V DC to operate, so the control board depends on a healthy house battery. A big fixed-speed compressor means a heavy startup surge, and a soft start or a strong pedestal is wise. The 50 dB claim is louder than the TOSOT's 43 dB.

Compared with the Gidrox it offers more cooling and less documentation about the heating figure. Check the 12V feed after any battery work and wash the filter monthly.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A real heat pump quotes heating close to its cooling figure, like the Gidrox 13,500 BTU with 12,000 BTU of heat or the TOSOT's 16,000 BTU with 12,500 BTU. A unit with a large cooling number and a tiny heating number is an air conditioner with a token heater. Compare the two figures before buying.

Heating BTU figures are quoted at mild outdoor temperatures. As the air nears freezing, a heat pump has less heat to move and its output falls, and it spends time in defrost cycles. The 15,000 BTU unit with an automatic defrost function and an electric backup element addresses this directly. Plan a furnace for anything colder, and do not let a high heating figure on a listing talk you out of that plan, since the number was measured in the mild conditions that flatter any heat pump.

A 115V unit like the Gidrox 13,500 BTU or the TOSOT needs shore power or a generator. A 12V or 48V unit runs from batteries but needs heavy cable and a large bank. The 48V Gidrox draws a quarter of the current of a 12V unit for the same power, which simplifies wiring in a 48V system. For a conventional trailer with a 12V house system, the practical choices are the 115V units, since converting a whole electrical system to 48V costs far more than the air conditioner.

In cool, damp air the outdoor coil frosts, and the unit periodically reverses to melt it. That produces water, which must drain freely, or it freezes and cracks a pan. An automatic defrost function and a clear drain path matter more in a heat pump than in a cooling-only unit.

A heat pump may run for hours overnight in mild weather, so a quiet claim matters. The Gidrox and TOSOT quote 43 dB, the Arsenda 50 dB and the 48V unit 40 dB in sleep mode. Defrost cycles add a brief thump, so a lower claim is a minimum, not a guarantee.

Dual-rotary and variable designs reduce vibration and improve efficiency, which matters when a heat pump runs for long periods. A dual-rotary 15,000 BTU unit lists this, while the fixed-speed TOSOT and Arsenda surge at startup. If you run on a generator, the compressor type decides whether a soft start is needed.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heating capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared quoted heating against cooling, from the Gidrox 13,500 BTU's 12,000 BTU of heat to the 48V unit's 11,000 BTU. A genuine heat pump has heating near its cooling rating. We treated all figures as mild-weather numbers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cold-weather features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for defrost functions, backup elements and published operating ranges. The 15,000 BTU unit scored for its automatic defrost and element. Others were credited for transition-season design.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power system
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched voltage class, 115V, 12V or 48V, to likely use. Battery units were judged on wiring demands. Dual-power units were flagged for needing a 12V feed.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and airflow
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 40 to 50 dB maker claims and airflow in CFM and cubic meters per hour. A heat pump runs long, so quiet counted. We converted airflow units for comparison.

howWeEvaluated.title: Documentation
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how clearly each listing described heat, power and defrost. Clear specifications scored higher. Mixed or vague listings were marked down.

maintenance.why: A heat pump moves air through the same coil in both modes. A clogged filter hurts heating and cooling.
Defrost water must drain. A frozen drain can crack the pan, so clear leaves and debris from the drain holes in the base and confirm water runs freely when you pour a cup into the pan.
Cracked sealant leaks cold air in winter and water in summer.
Battery-powered units draw high current. A loose lug runs hot.
A failed reversing valve is easier to find early. Compare vent temperature with the maker's claim.

faq.q: How cold can an RV heat pump work?
faq.a: Output falls steadily as the air nears freezing, and the unit spends more time in defrost cycles. Treat the quoted heating as a mild-weather number and plan on a furnace for colder nights. A thermometer at the vent in the first cool morning of the season tells you what your unit really delivers, and that figure is the one to plan around.

faq.q: Is a heat pump cheaper to run than a heater?
faq.a: In mild weather, yes. Makers claim 65 to 75 percent less energy than resistive heat, and the physics supports a large saving. The advantage shrinks in the cold. The saving is largest when the heat pump runs steadily at a gentle speed, and smallest when a cold, damp night forces constant defrost cycles.

faq.q: Can a heat pump replace a furnace?
faq.a: Not in freezing weather. It complements a furnace, covering spring and fall mornings and saving propane. Think of it as the first stage of heating, with the furnace as the second stage that takes over when the outdoor temperature drops.

faq.q: Why does my heat pump make water?
faq.a: In heating mode it defrosts the outdoor coil periodically, which melts ice into water. A clear drain path prevents freezing and leaks. If you see a puddle under the unit in cold weather, that is usually normal defrost water, but a puddle inside the coach is a sign of a blocked pan or a failed seal.

faq.q: What does 48V mean for an RV air conditioner?
faq.a: The unit runs from a 48V battery system, drawing a quarter of the current of a 12V unit for the same power. It needs a 48V system, which is uncommon in standard trailers.

faq.q: Do heat pump models cost much more?
faq.a: They usually cost more than a cooling-only unit of the same size, because they carry a reversing valve and a more capable coil. The payback comes in propane and furnace runtime, and it is slow if you camp mostly in summer. For a rig that lives in spring and fall conditions, the saving shows up quickly in fuel and in the quiet of not lighting a furnace.
